title: Salman Khan Has Never Read a Script — And He's Made 100 Films
excerpt: The Bollywood megastar's candid Variety India confession sparks debate about instinct vs. craft — and what it means for his upcoming slate
body:
# Salman Khan Has Never Read a Script — And He's Made 100 Films

Only Bhai could drop this confession with a straight face and have absolutely nobody question it.

In a candid interview with Variety India that's been ricocheting across Bollywood Twitter all week, Salman Khan casually revealed that he has never — not once, not ever — read a film script in his entire career. Over 100 films. Thirty-five-plus years. Zero scripts read.

"I've never read a script in my entire life. I have written them," Khan told the interviewer, with the kind of matter-of-fact confidence that only a man who once launched a franchise by removing his shirt can muster.

The Narration Method

Instead of poring over bound screenplays like his contemporaries, Khan prefers to hear stories directly from writers and directors. It's an oral tradition approach to commercial filmmaking — he wants to understand the narrator's vision, their passion, their conviction. If the storytelling grabs him in the room, he's in. If it doesn't, no number of rewrites will change his mind.

It's a method that sounds reckless on paper. But then, that's rather the point — there is no paper.

For the bigger career calls, Khan consults his father, the legendary screenwriter Salim Khan, one half of the Salim-Javed partnership that essentially invented the modern Bollywood blockbuster with Sholay and Deewaar. When your dad wrote the template for Hindi cinema's golden age, you've got a pretty good script consultant on speed dial.

The Debate: Instinct vs. Craft

The confession has ignited a spirited debate in industry circles. Supporters point to Khan's extraordinary instinct — the man who greenlit Bajrangi Bhaijaan (a cross-border drama that made grown men weep) and the Tiger franchise (which turned him into India's answer to Jason Bourne) clearly has a nose for what works. His Dabangg series alone proved that sometimes vibes beat three-act structure.

Critics, however, see the admission as exhibit A in explaining Khan's recent box office inconsistency. Films like Radhe and Kisi Ka Bhai Kisi Ki Jaan left audiences wondering if anyone involved had read the script — turns out the lead star definitely hadn't.

What's Coming Next

Khan's upcoming slate suggests the instinct remains sharp. He's currently deep in production on Maatrubhumi, an ambitious war drama set during the 2020 Galwan Valley clash between Indian and Chinese forces. Originally slated for earlier release, the film has been pushed to June 2026 — reportedly due to a combination of censorship concerns and extensive reshoots to get the battle sequences right. For a man who doesn't read scripts, he's apparently quite particular about execution.

Beyond that, Khan has a superhero film with the acclaimed director duo Raj & DK (of The Family Man fame), with shooting set to begin in October 2026 and production handled by his brother-in-law Atul Agnihotri. And there's an untitled project pairing him with South superstar Nayanthara, directed by Telugu hitmaker Vamshi Paidipally, eyeing an Eid 2027 release — because Salman Khan and Eid remain Bollywood's most reliable calendar appointment.

The NRI Angle

For the diaspora, this revelation lands differently. Salman Khan is arguably the single biggest NRI draw in Bollywood — his Eid releases are global events, the kind of films that fill multiplexes from Edison, New Jersey to Southall, London. NRI fans have been debating the confession with particular intensity, many wondering aloud whether the script-free approach explains why some recent releases felt undercooked while earlier films hit so hard.

"This explains everything about Race 3," one Reddit user on r/BollyBlindsNGossip wrote, in a comment that racked up thousands of upvotes.

But here's the thing about Salman Khan: he's never been about the screenplay. He's about the event, the spectacle, the promise of a good time. He's the star you show up for regardless of the plot summary. And if Maatrubhumi delivers the patriotic war epic its premise promises, nobody will care whether he read the script — they'll be too busy booking IMAX tickets from Houston to Sydney.

In an industry increasingly obsessed with "content-driven cinema," Salman Khan remains gloriously, stubbornly himself: a star who trusts his gut over the page. At 60, with a filmography that reads like a history of Bollywood itself, maybe he's earned the right.

After all, he's never read a script. And he's still Bhai.
